3.rendering: Renders κράτιστε as 'most honored Theophilus' rather than flattening to 'dear' or 'excellent.' The honorific keeps the social weight of a patron dedication visible — Theophilus is being publicly honored in writing, the way first-century dedications worked.
3.tradeOff: A modern reader may not immediately register 'most honored' as a status-tier address rather than warm courtesy, but anything weaker (dear/respected) drains the honor-transaction the original would have signaled.

3.rendering: Renders παρηκολουθηκότι as 'having traced the whole course of it carefully from the start,' unpacking the verb's investigative force rather than collapsing to 'having investigated' or 'having followed.' Keeps Luke's claim to thorough source-work visible.
3.tradeOff: Slightly longer than a one-word gloss; gains the historian's posture the verb carries.

4.rendering: Renders ἀσφάλεια concretely as 'how firm the ground is beneath the things you were taught' — keeps the spatial/foundational metaphor instead of abstracting to 'certainty' or 'truth.' The reader feels something to stand on.
4.tradeOff: More words than 'the certainty of what you were taught'; the image is worth it because Luke's whole prologue is an argument for solid footing.

7.rendering: Renders the childlessness as a plain physical fact ('Elizabeth could not have children, and by now both of them were old') with no moral or theological coloring. Pairs with v.25's vindication so the chapter never lets barrenness read as divine judgment.
7.tradeOff: None — the text itself refuses the shame framing; translation must not reintroduce it.

9.rendering: Adds 'Out of a whole lifetime, this was his one turn' to land the once-in-a-lifetime honor of being chosen by lot to burn incense. Without it, modern readers hear only 'he went in and burned incense' and miss why this moment carries such weight.
9.tradeOff: An explicit amplification that the Greek leaves to cultural assumption; justified because the encounter with Gabriel only lands at full force if the reader feels the rarity of the priestly assignment.

15.rendering: Keeps 'wine or strong drink' (σίκερα) as a doubled phrase and frames it as a binding 'must never' rather than a generic 'will not.' The Nazirite/prophetic vow flavor stays audible.
15.tradeOff: Modern English doesn't use 'strong drink' colloquially anymore; preserved because collapsing to 'alcohol' loses the biblical-vow register and the echo of Samson/Samuel.

17.rendering: Renders 'turn the hearts of parents back to their children' rather than 'fathers to their children.' The Malachi quotation in context is about family reconciliation broadly; 'parents' lets the verse land for mothers in the room too without distorting the Hebrew.
17.tradeOff: Loses the literal πατέρων = 'fathers'; gains accuracy for a household-reconciliation promise that modern readers in single-mother households can hear themselves inside of.

25.rendering: Renders ὄνειδος as 'the shame I carried in front of everyone' — names the shame as a social load that other people imposed on Elizabeth, not as a moral stain she deserved. Vindicates her without moralizing infertility.
25.tradeOff: Slightly more interpretive than 'reproach' or 'disgrace'; needed to keep the harm-history warning honored (the text must not be allowed to read as 'God finally fixed her defect').

26.rendering: Adds 'a place no one important had ever heard of' to Nazareth. The original audience knew Nazareth as a backwater of 200–400 peasants; modern readers know it only as a Christmas-card name. The amplification restores the marginality that makes God's choice scandalous.
26.tradeOff: An explicit gloss that the Greek leaves implicit. Justified because the reversal theme of the whole chapter only begins to operate if Nazareth registers as nowhere.

27.rendering: Amplifies the betrothal note with the full social stakes: 'The pledge was binding, as good as marriage… For a girl in her position, a pregnancy now would look like only one thing, betrayal, and a betrothed girl found pregnant could be denounced, cast off, even stoned.' This is the offense the original audience felt and modern readers miss entirely.
27.tradeOff: A heavy amplification — easily the longest in the chapter — that lengthens the verse considerably and risks reading as commentary. Kept because the friction is non-negotiable per the must-land brief: Mary's 'yes' has no weight unless the danger is on the page.

34.rendering: Adds 'She knew what such a pregnancy would cost her, and still she stayed in the conversation' after Mary's question. Frames her virtue as faith-response under known danger, not naïveté or merely physical virginity.
34.tradeOff: An interpretive expansion the Greek leaves implicit; justified by the harm-history concern that this text has been weaponized to valorize physical virginity rather than Mary's costly faith.

35.rendering: Renders ἐπισκιάσει with the tabernacle allusion made explicit: 'the power of the Most High will settle over you, the way God's presence once filled the tent of meeting.' Modern readers don't hear the Exodus 40 echo from 'overshadow' alone.
35.tradeOff: An exegetical gloss inside the running text rather than a footnote; warranted because the conception scene's whole register is Shekinah-language and the echo carries the theology.

38.rendering: Renders ἰδοὺ ἡ δούλη κυρίου as 'I am the Lord's servant. I give myself to this' — separates the self-identification from a verbal handover, making Mary's consent active rather than passive ('let it be done to me').
38.tradeOff: Slightly more agentive than the Greek middle-voice; preserved because Mary's virtue per the brief is her faith-response, and the traditional 'let it be done' has hardened into passivity.

45.rendering: Renders τελείωσις as 'brought to its full completion' rather than 'fulfilled.' The verbal noun keeps the sense of a process being driven all the way to its end, which Luke uses programmatically.
45.tradeOff: Marginally heavier than 'fulfilled'; gains the trajectory.

46.rendering: Opens with 'Everything in me celebrates God. / My spirit dances over the One who saves me' — chooses kinetic verbs (celebrates/dances) over the ecclesial 'magnifies/rejoices.' Holds Mary's song as embodied joy, not liturgical formula.
46.tradeOff: Loses the lectionary cadence that older translations carry; gains a Mary who actually sounds like a peasant girl bursting into song.

48.rendering: Renders ταπείνωσιν as 'a servant girl, a nobody.' Doubles the term — first the social role, then the social value — so the reversal hits both registers. 'Low estate' or 'humble state' is too genteel for what Mary is naming.
48.tradeOff: 'A nobody' is a colloquial choice that some readers will find too informal; justified because Mary is naming her actual status in a Galilean village, not striking a humility-pose.

51.rendering: Breaks the Greek aorist string into three short clauses: 'He has acted. In raw strength. With his arm.' The staccato rhythm carries the prophetic-perfect force that a single flowing sentence would smooth away.
51.tradeOff: Heavily unusual punctuation for a biblical text; gains the percussive weight the aorist verbs carry as Mary moves from personal to cosmic reversal.

52.rendering: Renders καθεῖλεν as 'dragged the powerful down from their thrones' rather than the genteel 'brought down' or 'put down.' The verb is forcible and the social-reversal brief demands the violence of the verb stay audible.
52.tradeOff: 'Dragged' is stronger than the lexicon-minimum gloss; chosen because the Magnificat is political and softening it has been the long historical pattern.

53.rendering: Keeps 'the hungry he has filled with good things, and the rich he has sent away with empty hands' as a sharp economic reversal — no spiritualizing of 'hungry' to 'spiritually hungry,' no abstraction of 'rich' to 'self-satisfied.' The Jubilee/economic edge is preserved.
53.tradeOff: None — the brief is explicit that this is concrete economic reversal and must read that way.

60.rendering: Renders Elizabeth's intervention as 'But his mother cut in. "No," she said. "He is to be called John." She would not be talked out of it.' Amplifies her agency over the naming — a woman overriding family convention is the shock the original community felt.
60.tradeOff: Adds a sentence ('She would not be talked out of it') the Greek doesn't have; justified because the must-land brief calls for the gender shock to be felt and modern readers won't catch it from a flat 'his mother answered.'

63.rendering: Adds 'to everyone's astonishment' before Zechariah writes 'His name is John.' Makes the breach of naming convention visible as a public surprise rather than a quiet detail.
63.tradeOff: Mild amplification; preserves the dramatic tension Bovon identifies (will Zechariah override Elizabeth or confirm her?).

68.rendering: Renders ἐποίησεν λύτρωσιν as 'has come to his people and bought them back' rather than 'redeemed' or 'visited and redeemed.' Keeps the ransom-from-bondage image audible; 'redeemed' has gone abstract in modern usage.
68.tradeOff: 'Bought back' is concrete commercial language some readers will find jarring; that concreteness is exactly what the Greek carries and what 'redeemed' has lost.

78.rendering: Renders σπλάγχνα ἐλέους as 'the gut-deep mercy of our God' — keeps the visceral organ-language ('bowels of mercy') without the archaism. Mercy here is bodily, not a courtroom transaction.
78.tradeOff: 'Gut-deep' is colloquial; chosen because the Greek points to viscera, and any abstraction ('tender mercy,' 'compassion') flattens the embodied register.

78.rendering: Renders ἀνατολή as 'the Dawn from on high will break over us' — keeps the sunrise image (and the messianic-shoot resonance behind it) rather than 'the rising sun' or a vague 'morning light.' Pairs with v.79's people sitting in darkness.
78.tradeOff: Capitalized 'Dawn' makes the messianic edge more pointed than the Greek strictly requires; preserved because the image is the engine of the Benedictus's closing couplet.

80.rendering: Renders ἀναδείξεως αὐτοῦ as 'until the day he stepped into the open before Israel' rather than 'until the day of his showing/manifestation.' Keeps the moment as a public emergence with named audience; preserves the unresolved 'what then will this child become?' tension by closing on a deferred reveal.
80.tradeOff: Slightly more cinematic than the Greek's nominal phrase; gains a closing image that holds chapter 1's narrative cliffhanger until chapter 3.
